segment_labels.text:
The grinding wheel whined through a merchant’s blade, and Kesh counted. Six seconds against the stone, water hissing, then lift. Turn. Six seconds more. His hands were scarred in pale crescents from six years at this wheel, but the count came from older than that. Eighteen strokes per side. Nineteen would blue the edge. He didn’t need to look.

Around him the eighth forge breathed: bellows, doors, apprentices shouting at quench buckets. Cold from Vhalun’s high streets leaked through the open bay and fought the coal smoke. Kesh put the merchant’s blade on the rack, checked the bevel with his thumbnail, and whispered, “Twelve copper. Mother’s account needs four hundred before spring.” He wiped his hands on his apron.

Journeyman evaluation was three weeks out. If he passed, the guild bond went up, and Master Oren could advance wages against it. That was the plan. It had to work. The debt collector’s last note was pinned inside his boot, folded thin enough to forget except when he walked.

“Mather,” he called to the second-year sweeping scale, “is the coal delivery in?”

The boy shrugged. “Loading yard had crates, not coal.”

Kesh hung his apron by the grinding wheel. The loading yard lay two steps down, cut into the mountain rock. Four men from the eastern dock were unloading eight crates from a cart. The crates were long, iron-banded, built for weight. Kesh counted them automatically. Eight.

He came down the stone stairs. The eastern dock men set the last crate against the forge’s trade wall. Stenciled on each side, in fresh black paint: IX-M. The guild’s mark was a bell over crossed hammers. This wasn’t theirs.

Oren stood by the cart, hands behind his back. He wore his public face, the one he used at guild auctions. When he saw Kesh, the face didn’t change.

“Master,” Kesh said. “That seal isn’t the guild’s.”

Oren looked at the crates as if he’d just noticed them. “It’s the buyer’s mark. They run their own inventory.” Then he turned to the dock foreman. “Eight crates, two hundredweight total. At the flat rate.”

The foreman nodded. “Eastern dock’ll send the rest of the payment tonight.”

Oren didn’t look at Kesh again. “You’re at the grinding wheel until third bell.”

Kesh stayed where he was. “What buyer uses a guild seal like that? The IX—”

Oren’s hand came up, one finger. “That mark means the buyer paid for the stock before it left. On time. In full.” His finger dropped. “Wheel. Third bell.”

Kesh counted Oren’s steps back to the master’s office. Twelve. A normal number. But Oren had not answered the question.

He went back to the grinding wheel, but the number didn’t settle. Eight crates. Two hundredweight of arms-grade stock, if the weight held. But the eighth forge didn’t cast arms. They made merchant’s blades, plowshares, gate hinges. Small batch. So why was Oren signing shipment in flat rate instead of per piece?

At the second bell, Kesh took the tally slate to the coal shed. It was a narrow room behind the quench line, where the sacks were weighed and recorded. He flipped through the ledger. Last quarter, the forge burned forty-two sacks. This quarter, through eight weeks, the number was sixty-one. Nearly doubled. He looked at the forge output log on the same shelf.

Blades, hinges, plated locks. Piece count was flat. Worse than flat. A little down.

He spoke to Oren at the cooling rack. “The coal account has doubled this quarter.”

Oren didn’t look up from the quench barrel. “Coal north of the pass is four silver a sack now. Last fall it was two and a half. You feed the same fires, you pay more.”

“But the ledger says sacks, not silver.”

Now Oren looked at him. His eyes moved over Kesh’s face like he was pricing it. “Then read it in silver. The forge takes no sides. It takes payment. You want to count something, count your strokes at the wheel.”

Kesh’s jaw tightened. “If the forge is spending heat it isn’t selling, that’s—”

“That’s math for masters.” Oren dipped a probe into the quench water. “If you finish the merchant’s blade and the two hinges by fourth bell, there’s a chance we discuss your journeyman seat. If you keep asking about coal, there isn’t.”

The probe came out dripping. Oren walked away.

Kesh stood there. The quench water stilled. Behind the barrel, on the rough stone wall, there was a smear of chalk. He hadn’t noticed it before. It looked like tally marks, almost, but muddled by steam. He didn’t look long.

He went back to the grinding wheel. The plan was already cracking. He needed Oren’s recommendation. He needed the advance. Without it, the debt collector would take the house before spring. His mother had said so in her last letter. The paper was thin and reused. That was the message.

But the numbers at the forge didn’t add. He counted what the forge made: in the previous five days, the forge sold four merchant blades, eight hinge pairs, three locks. The forge’s coal ledger said two sacks a day. The output log said one fire’s worth. That was the problem. The forge was running two fires, but only one set of products.

By the fourth bell, he had finished the merchant’s blade and two hinges. He stacked them on the trade shelf. Oren didn’t come to check. The other apprentices filed out. Kesh stood by the quench barrel. The chalk smear behind it had dried, and now he could see it clearly. It was a tally. Seven short marks, then a long line through four. A night-shift count? He didn’t know.

He did know that asking had already cost him. Oren’s threat about the journeyman seat was real. One more question and the recommendation could disappear. The house would go before spring. His mother would move into his aunt’s single room, or worse. The collector’s note in his boot said exactly what the house was worth. He had memorized it.

Kesh took the tally slate from the coal shed and turned to the output log. He didn’t ask anyone. He set the log on the cooling rack and ran his finger down the columns. Sold count, material in, coal burned, losses. He started forming another count. Eight crates at two hundredweight total. If the stock was arms-grade, one crate could hold thirty long barrels. Eight crates. Two hundredweight. That was heat no one had paid for in the output log.

He closed the log. The chalk tally behind the quench barrel sat in the corner of his eye. He wanted to wipe it off the wall. Instead he picked up a bit of chalk from the floor and held it over his own slate.

The door to the master’s office opened. Oren’s boots stopped on the stone. “You’ve finished the pieces,” Oren said. “Good.”

Kesh didn’t turn around. He counted Oren’s steps. Five to the cooling rack.

“I’m in the tally,” Kesh said. “The numbers don’t match.”

Oren said nothing. Kesh could hear him breathing. Then Oren said, “Coal is at four silver a sack. Last quarter’s extra didn’t buy what you think it bought. Put the slate down, Kesh.”

Kesh held the chalk over the slate. His hand didn’t shake. That was the training. But he didn’t put it down.

In the quiet, Kesh counted the beats between Oren’s indrawn breath and the next words. He got to three.

“Your mother’s debt,” Oren said. “I can advance it. Before spring.”

Kesh finally turned. Oren stood by the cooling rack, arms loose, his public face gone. The offer hung between them.

Kesh looked at the chalk in his hand. The tally marks on the wall. The closed output log.

He didn’t ask what the advance would cost.

He turned back to the slate. The next thing he meant to write was a single number.
